This is the brake, located precisely. T1 removes only head 3's response to the end-of-prompt value direction: a rank-1 change carrying 0.7% of that head's weight energy. It gives +25.7 ± 3.4 points (66 wrong→right, only 8 right→wrong). Accuracy rises from 18.6% to 44.2%, cut-offs fall from 28% to 7%, and mean answer length from 346 to 247 tokens.

That is clearly better than damping the whole head (×0.2: +18.6) on the same problems. So the harm is not head 3 as such but its amplified pass-through of the large end-of-prompt value vector to every answer token, and the head's other, useful function is now kept.

Next I make the edit clean, check whether there are more brakes of the same kind, and understand what it removes:

1. **DEV-only direction.** The V_last direction came from the pass-1 activations. If pass 1 included HOLDOUT problems, I rebuild the direction from DEV problems only, so that HOLDOUT stays untouched.
2. **What the removed write does.** I characterise head 3's write along that input direction: its size, its massive-dimension share, its alignment with the spike and with D1, its effect after the post-norm, and a logit lens on a few curated tokens.
3. **Same anomaly elsewhere.** I scan all 104 heads for a gain on their own layer's end-of-prompt value direction that is unusually high relative to the head's average gain. In L11 the siblings sit at 0.6–0.9× and head 3 at 1.37×. A planted brake of the same kind elsewhere would show up as a similar outlier.

The model-wide scan changes how to read the anomaly. Head 3's gain along its layer's end-of-prompt value direction (1.37× its average gain) is only at the 90th percentile of all 104 heads (median 1.03). All four L18 heads respond far more strongly (2.1–4.3×), and L18 also has a very large end-of-prompt value (7.3× the answer mean, like L11's 7.4×). By weight statistics alone, head 3 does not stand out on this measure, and L18's uniform pattern across all heads looks like a natural sink-value mechanism.

What does stand out is where head 3's removed write lands. Its direction w is concentrated (65% of its energy in 50 dimensions), unrelated to the spike (cos 0.12) and to D1 (cos 0.00). L11's post-attention norm amplifies it 2.6× more than a typical direction (gain 40 against a median of 15). That is the reverse of the harmless spike, which sat in dimensions the norm discards.

The most telling test of a planted brake is conditionality: is the large end-of-prompt value at L11 specific to math prompts? Earlier passes contain non-math prompts (pass 7 had a poem), so I look for stored end-of-prompt hidden states at L11 input (index 11) for non-math texts. I list what each teacher-forced pass returned (hidden-state layers, text labels) before comparing math and non-math V_last.

fwd_2 is a 500-text teacher-forced pass with hidden states including index 11 (the L11 input). Its texts come in groups G1–G5, which my notes used for math-vs-other contrasts. I print a sample of each group (start and end of the text) and confirm which hidden indices exist. Then I can compare the end-of-prompt value at L11 between math prompts and the other groups.

If |V_last| at L11 (and head 3's write of it) is much larger for math prompts than for the other groups, the broadcast is math-conditional, which would mark a planted brake. If it is the same for all prompts, the harm is a general oversized pass-through that happens to hurt reasoning.
